AI features fail when teams jump from a vague user pain to a model or framework without defining the job, simplest baseline, constraints, success evidence, and acceptable failure behavior.

items.en: Turn a user workflow and pain into a concrete product objective.
Define a non-AI or simpler-system baseline that the proposed AI feature must beat.
Separate product success criteria from model or system implementation choices.
State constraints, out-of-scope behavior, unacceptable failures, and operational trade-offs before architecture selection.
Produce an evaluation contract and milestone plan that make later architecture changes falsifiable.

tasks.en: Given a request to build an AI knowledge assistant, write the user, pain, value proposition, baseline, success criteria, constraints, and unacceptable failures before naming a model or framework.
Explain what evidence would cause you to reject AI entirely or keep a lexical/manual workflow.
Identify which decisions belong to product framing and which belong to later system design.

pass_condition.en: Skip guided material only if the learner produces a concrete, measurable frame whose success criteria and baseline can drive later evaluation and architecture decisions.

locator.en: Product Design lesson sections "Background", "Value proposition", "Objectives", "Solution", and "Feasibility"

purpose.en: Build the product-first sequence from user pain through objectives, alternatives, constraints, out-of-scope behavior, and feasibility.

purpose.en: Connect product framing to foundation-model suitability, expectations, milestones, and lifecycle cost.

Eliminate infeasible models before optimizing soft preferences.
Compare task quality, latency, cost, deployment, and operational constraints on representative evidence.
Explain build-versus-buy and hosted-versus-self-hosted trade-offs where relevant.
Record uncertainty and identify evidence that would change the decision.
Re-evaluate the choice when constraints or workload change.

tasks.en: Given several model candidates, explain what evidence is needed before choosing one.
Separate hard constraints from optimization goals.
Explain why a public benchmark winner may be the wrong production choice.
Describe how latency, cost, privacy, and task-specific quality enter one decision.

pass_condition.en: Skip guided material only if the learner can produce a constraint-first selection process and defend a choice using task-specific evaluation evidence rather than generic model reputation.

Complete the constraint-first model-selection decision and sensitivity test.

items.en: Replace synthetic profiles with measured results from two or more real candidates on a versioned local eval set.
Change one important product constraint and observe whether the decision changes.
Produce a hard-constraint filter before ranking candidates.

Compare candidates using task-specific quality plus operational evidence.
Record rejected candidates and why they were rejected.

body.en: Re-run the selection process for a different workload, such as batch classification or an offline/private deployment, and explain which criteria change.

Model behavior depends on the full inference context, not only prompt wording. Useful systems must select, organize, trim, retrieve, and compact instructions, examples, external data, tool information, history, and state under a finite attention budget.

diagnostic.en: Given a vague system prompt, rewrite it with a clear task, separated instructions and supplied context, and one justified example; explain what failure the change is meant to fix.

locator.en: Chapter 5 "Prompt Engineering" — "Introduction to Prompting" (p. 212), "System Prompt and User Prompt" (p. 215), and "Prompt Engineering Best Practices" (from p. 220)

purpose.en: Patch only the instruction-design skill needed to distinguish prompt wording from broader context selection and management.

items.en: Inventory the context presented to a model call, including instructions, task input, examples, retrieved data, tool definitions/results, history, and persisted state.
Identify context that is necessary, redundant, stale, conflicting, low-signal, or too expensive.
Define a context budget and selection policy from product and evaluation requirements rather than maximum context-window size.
Compare up-front context loading with just-in-time or progressive retrieval.
Design trimming, summarization, or compaction while preserving goals, constraints, decisions, and unresolved state.
Measure quality, latency, token/cost, and failure behavior under controlled context ablations.
Version context inputs and selection rules so regressions can be reproduced.

tasks.en: For a RAG assistant, list every context component that reaches the model and identify which components can become stale, noisy, conflicting, or oversized.
Design an ablation that tests whether more retrieved/history context improves or hurts the same evaluation set.
Explain the difference between prompt engineering, retrieval, context engineering, context-window mechanics, and memory.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design a controlled context experiment, explain the boundary with adjacent competencies, and make an evidence-based context-selection decision.

locator.en: Sections "Context engineering vs. prompt engineering", "The anatomy of effective context", "Context retrieval and agentic search", and "Context engineering for long-horizon tasks"

purpose.en: Establish context as the full inference state and introduce high-signal selection, just-in-time retrieval, and compaction under a finite attention budget.

locator.en: Section "We made repository knowledge the system of record"

purpose.en: Study a production pattern that keeps a small stable map in context while moving deeper knowledge into navigable external sources.

Compare at least three context configurations on the same Knowledge Assistant evaluation set, including one minimal high-signal configuration, one broad/noisy configuration, and one dynamically selected or compacted configuration.

items.en: Add stale or distracting retrieved/history context and measure whether quality degrades.

Compare always-loaded context with just-in-time retrieval or progressive disclosure.
Compact a long conversation/state record and verify whether goals, constraints, decisions, and unresolved work survive.
A versioned context inventory records component source, selection rule, and approximate size.
At least three context configurations are compared on a fixed evaluation contract.
Quality is reported alongside token/context size and latency/cost where measurable.
At least one stale, distracting, conflicting, or long-history failure is tested.
The decision records what context is deliberately excluded, loaded just in time, or compacted and why.

body.en: Redesign the context policy for a different application such as support triage, coding assistance, or document analysis where the source mix, freshness, history, and tool context differ.

Downstream systems need predictable contracts, but valid JSON or schema-conforming output does not guarantee semantic correctness. Engineers must design response schemas, handle refusal and incomplete states, validate business invariants deterministically, and version the contract safely.

items.en: Design a small JSON Schema or equivalent typed contract from downstream consumer needs.
Distinguish valid JSON, schema validity, semantic or business validity, and task correctness.
Use required fields, enums, nullability, and additional-property policy intentionally.
Explain constrained generation conceptually and identify provider-specific schema subsets or limitations.
Handle normal output, refusal or unavailable state, incomplete or truncated output, and schema-compliant but semantically invalid values separately.
Validate semantic invariants deterministically after generation.
Version output schemas and identify breaking versus compatible changes.
Compare free-form parsing, JSON-only output, and schema-constrained output on reliability and operational cost where supported.

tasks.en: Design a response schema for a cited Knowledge Assistant answer and explain which properties belong in the schema versus deterministic semantic validation.
Explain why schema-valid output can still be wrong for the task.
Describe how refusal, incomplete output, and a schema migration should be represented without silently treating them as normal success.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design a typed response contract, separate schema validity from semantic correctness, handle non-happy paths, and reason about schema evolution.

locator.en: Sections "How to use Structured Outputs", "Safe Structured Outputs", "Under the hood", and "Constrained decoding"

purpose.en: Understand schema-constrained generation, refusal and incomplete-output handling, and the difference between valid JSON and schema adherence.

locator.en: Sections "JSON schema support", "Structured outputs versus function calling", "Best practices", and "Limitations"

purpose.en: Compare another provider's schema subset, semantic-validation guidance, and the boundary between structured final responses and tool execution.

locator.en: Sections "Properties", "Required Properties", and "Additional Properties"

purpose.en: Ground basic object-contract semantics in the schema standard rather than provider-specific syntax.

text.en: Take one existing Knowledge Assistant response and convert it into a typed contract, then list at least three semantic invariants that the schema cannot prove.
Add a versioned structured response contract to the Knowledge Assistant, implement deterministic semantic validation and non-happy-path handling, then compare it with the prior free-form baseline.

items.en: Compare free-form parsing, JSON-only output, and schema-constrained output on the same evaluation set when the provider supports them.
Inject a schema-valid but semantically invalid response and verify deterministic validation rejects or routes it appropriately.
Exercise refusal or unavailable and incomplete or truncated paths instead of mapping them to a normal answer.
Change the schema once and classify the migration as compatible or breaking for the downstream consumer.
A versioned schema is tied to a concrete downstream consumer requirement.
Contract tests distinguish malformed transport, schema failure, semantic failure, refusal or unavailable state, incomplete output, and task failure.
Deterministic semantic invariants are documented and enforced outside the model.
Provider and supported-schema constraints are recorded.
One schema migration decision identifies compatibility and consumer impact.
Reliability and operational evidence are compared against the prior free-form baseline.

body.en: Redesign the response contract for a different consumer such as a UI card, workflow API, or batch export and explain which fields, invariants, and compatibility rules change.

Tool-enabled AI systems cross a boundary from model suggestions into real application behavior. Engineers must design clear tool contracts, validate model-generated arguments, enforce policy in deterministic code, handle failures and retries safely, shape tool results for context, and evaluate raw tool traces rather than only final answers.

diagnostic.en: Given a mutating create-ticket operation, define request validation, success/error responses, timeout behavior, retryable versus non-retryable failures, and how duplicate retries avoid duplicate side effects.

locator.en: Sections "Reducing client complexity with idempotent API design" and "Retries and semantic equivalence"

purpose.en: Patch the API contract, error, retry, and idempotency reasoning required for safe tool execution without requiring the full API/service-design curriculum.

items.en: Design a small, distinct tool surface from a user or workflow need rather than exposing every backend endpoint.
Define clear tool names, descriptions, schemas, parameter semantics, and result/error contracts.
Validate model-generated tool arguments before execution.
Keep identity, authorization, approval, and side-effect policy in deterministic application code that model output cannot override.
Handle success, validation errors, transient failures, timeouts, retries, and non-retryable failures.
Make mutating retries safe through explicit idempotency semantics.
Return concise task-relevant tool results rather than dumping backend payloads into model context.
Trace and evaluate tool selection, arguments, validation, execution, errors, retries, results, and final task outcome.
Distinguish failures caused by tool selection, malformed arguments, execution, permissions, result shaping, or post-tool reasoning.

tasks.en: Design one tool contract for a Knowledge Assistant workflow, including schema, validation, authorization boundary, result/error shapes, timeout, and retry behavior.
Explain why schema-valid model output is not authorization to execute a privileged action.

Design an evaluation that can detect a wrong tool choice even if the final answer happens to look correct.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design and evaluate a provider-independent tool boundary with deterministic validation, policy enforcement, safe retries, context-efficient results, and inspectable traces.

purpose.en: Connect tool-surface design, descriptions, result shaping, token efficiency, and raw-trace evaluation.

purpose.en: Make timeout/retry behavior safe for mutating operations through explicit idempotency semantics.

Add one justified tool-enabled Knowledge Assistant workflow, implement deterministic validation and execution controls, then evaluate realistic success, should-not-call, malformed, permission, timeout, retry, and result-shaping cases.

items.en: Compare a broad tool surface with a smaller task-oriented tool surface on the same evaluation tasks.

Identity, authorization, approval, and privileged side-effect controls are enforced outside model output.

Embeddings make semantic retrieval possible, but useful systems depend on query/document task fit, similarity behavior, model choice, normalization, domain mismatch, and measured comparison against simpler retrieval.

diagnostic.en: Given two short vectors, compute or explain dot product and cosine similarity and describe what normalization changes.

locator.en: Chapter 6 §6.3 "The vector space model for scoring", especially §6.3.1 "Dot products" and cosine similarity discussion

purpose.en: Patch only the vector-similarity mathematics needed to reason about embedding retrieval scores.

items.en: Explain what an embedding-based retriever represents and how similarity produces a ranking.
Distinguish symmetric similarity tasks from asymmetric query-to-document retrieval.
Choose query/document encoding and similarity behavior appropriate to the retrieval task.
Compare semantic retrieval with the same lexical baseline, corpus, relevance judgments, and query set.
Diagnose semantic retrieval failures such as domain mismatch, weak representations, normalization/scoring mistakes, and loss of exact lexical signals.

tasks.en: Explain the difference between embedding two similar sentences and embedding a short query against a longer document corpus.
Predict how cosine similarity changes when vector magnitude changes but direction does not.

pass_condition.en: Skip guided material only if the learner can reason about representation, similarity, asymmetric retrieval, and can evaluate semantic retrieval against a controlled lexical baseline.

body.en: Evaluate embedding retrieval on a new corpus whose queries differ in length or domain from the first project, and justify whether the same model, encoding strategy, and similarity function still fit.

Retrieval systems need a measurable baseline before semantic search, RAG, reranking, or agents can be justified. Engineers must be able to represent queries and documents, rank results, evaluate relevance, and diagnose lexical failure modes.

items.en: Build a lexical ranked-retrieval baseline over a real document collection.
Explain term weighting, document/query representations, scoring, and top-k ranking at an engineering level.
Create relevance judgments and measure retrieval quality separately from answer generation.
Diagnose misses caused by vocabulary mismatch, rare terms, document structure, filters, or stale content.
Use baseline evidence to decide whether semantic retrieval or another technique is justified.

tasks.en: Given a document collection and ten queries, describe a lexical baseline, relevance labels, ranking metric, and failure-analysis process.
Explain why returning documents containing all query terms is not the same as useful ranked retrieval.
For one failed query, identify evidence that would distinguish vocabulary mismatch from indexing or relevance-label problems.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can implement and evaluate a ranked lexical baseline, explain its scoring, and use failures to motivate the next retrieval change.

locator.en: Chapter 6 "Scoring, term weighting and the vector space model", especially §§6.2-6.3; Chapter 8 "Evaluation in information retrieval", especially ranked-retrieval evaluation

purpose.en: Learn term weighting, query/document vector scoring, ranking, relevance judgments, and retrieval evaluation.

locator.en: Chapter 6 "RAG and Agents" → "RAG" → "Retrieval Algorithms" (pp. 253-268, especially retrieval algorithms from p. 257)

purpose.en: Place term-based retrieval beside embedding-based retrieval inside modern AI application architecture.

Implement the Knowledge Assistant lexical baseline and record the corpus version, query set, relevance labels, top-k results, retrieval metric, latency, and failure taxonomy.

items.en: Change tokenization, stop-word handling, or term weighting and measure whether the same query set improves or regresses.

The learner can explain the scoring/ranking mechanism rather than only calling a search library.

Chunk boundaries determine what a retriever can find and what evidence reaches generation. Treating chunking as a framework default can hide boundary loss, duplicated context, broad noisy chunks, and corpus-structure mismatch.

items.en: Explain chunking as a retrieval and index representation decision rather than preprocessing boilerplate.
Compare chunking strategies while keeping the corpus, query set, relevance judgments, retriever, and evaluation definitions controlled.
Measure retrieval effects using ranking/recall evidence alongside latency, index size, and duplicated or wasted context.
Diagnose boundary loss, over-fragmentation, overly broad chunks, excessive overlap, and mismatch with document structure.
Choose a chunking strategy from measured behavior rather than a framework default.

tasks.en: Given long technical documents and a fixed retriever, design a fair experiment comparing three chunking strategies.
Explain how a chunk can improve Recall@K while making supplied context noisier.
Diagnose whether a missed answer is more likely caused by chunk boundaries, the retriever, or the relevance labels.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design and interpret a controlled chunking experiment and explain the retrieval/context trade-offs behind the result.

locator.en: Chapter 6 "RAG and Agents" → "Retrieval Optimization" (pp. 268-272)

purpose.en: Place data preparation and retrieval optimization inside the RAG pipeline rather than treating chunking as an isolated splitter API.

locator.en: Section 4.2 "RAG evaluation"

purpose.en: Study a controlled comparison where multiple chunking methods are evaluated while retrieval and generation components remain consistent; use the experimental pattern, not the proposed algorithm as a default.

text.en: Take five failed queries from the Knowledge Assistant and predict whether smaller, larger, overlapping, or structure-aware chunks should help before changing the index.
Compare at least three sensible chunking configurations on the same corpus/query/evaluation contract and produce a reproducible experiment record plus decision.

items.en: Sweep chunk size or boundary strategy while holding the retriever and query set fixed.
Compare overlap against duplicated-context and index-size cost rather than assuming more overlap is better.
Analyze at least one query slice where the aggregate winner is not the best strategy.
Exact splitter configurations and corpus/query-set versions are recorded.
At least three strategies are compared under a controlled evidence contract.
Retrieval metrics and operational/context costs are reported together.
Representative failures are classified by boundary, fragmentation, noise, overlap, or corpus-structure mismatch.
The chosen strategy and rejected alternatives are justified from measured evidence.

body.en: Redesign the chunking experiment for a structurally different corpus such as API docs, support tickets, or legal/policy documents and explain which assumptions from the first corpus no longer hold.

First-stage retrieval is optimized for candidate generation and scale, while a more expensive query-document scorer can improve ordering on a smaller candidate set. Reranking only helps if the needed evidence was retrieved in the first place and the quality gain justifies added latency and cost.

items.en: Separate candidate generation from final ranking and explain the different constraints on each stage.
Explain why first-stage candidate recall creates an upper bound on what a reranker can recover.
Add a more expensive query-document scorer to a real candidate set without changing the evaluation contract.
Measure ranking improvement and end-to-end retrieval latency across candidate-set sizes and query slices.
Decide whether reranking is justified and diagnose failures it cannot fix.

tasks.en: Explain why scoring every document with a cross-encoder-style model is usually impractical for a large corpus.
Given top-100 candidates with poor top-5 ordering, design a reranking experiment and select ranking/latency evidence.
Explain what a reranker can do when the relevant document is absent from the candidate set.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design a two-stage retrieval experiment, reason about candidate recall, and evaluate ranking gain against operational cost.

locator.en: Sections Retrieve & Re-Rank Pipeline; Retrieval: Bi-Encoder; and Re-Ranker: Cross-Encoder

purpose.en: Make the two-stage candidate-generation versus expensive pair-scoring architecture concrete while showing that the first stage may be lexical or dense.

locator.en: Chapter 8 "Evaluation in information retrieval", especially ranked-retrieval evaluation

purpose.en: Ground reranking decisions in ranking evidence rather than visual inspection of a few examples.

text.en: Inspect ten queries where a relevant item is present in the first-stage candidates but ranked too low; predict which can plausibly be fixed by reranking.
Add a reranking stage to the Knowledge Assistant, preserve the first-stage candidate list, sweep candidate-set size, and compare ranking quality plus end-to-end retrieval latency.

items.en: Sweep candidate-set size and measure candidate recall, final ranking quality, and latency.
Compare at least one slice where reranking helps with one where it cannot recover a first-stage miss.
Remove reranking and verify whether the observed quality gain is large enough to justify the extra stage.
The first-stage retriever/version and candidate-set size are recorded.
Candidate recall and final ranking quality are measured separately.
Ranking improvement is reported with latency/cost impact and query slices.
At least one unrecoverable first-stage miss is identified.
The decision to keep, change, or remove reranking is justified from evidence.

body.en: Apply the same two-stage reasoning to a different candidate generator such as lexical, dense, or hybrid retrieval and explain how the first-stage error profile changes the reranking experiment.

End-to-end answer quality can hide whether a RAG system failed at retrieval, context selection, generation, or evaluation itself. Reliable iteration requires component evidence, failure attribution, evaluator provenance, and regression cases.

items.en: Separate retrieval, supplied-context, generation, and end-to-end evaluation.
Choose retrieval metrics from explicit relevance judgments when available and pair them with answer/context evidence.
Diagnose whether a bad answer originates from missing evidence, poor ranking/context construction, or unfaithful/incorrect generation.
Use model-based evaluators only with explicit metric/rubric definitions, evaluator provenance, and human-reviewed calibration for important subjective judgments.
Convert important RAG failures into regression cases and make architecture or release decisions from the combined evidence.

tasks.en: Given a wrong RAG answer, design evidence that distinguishes retrieval failure from generation failure.
Explain why one aggregate RAG score cannot tell you which component to fix.
Describe how you would validate an LLM-based faithfulness or relevance evaluator before using it as a release signal.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design component-level RAG evaluation, attribute failures, and define trustworthy evaluator/release evidence.

locator.en: Abstract and framework sections describing retrieval context relevance/focus, generation faithfulness, and generation quality as distinct evaluation dimensions

purpose.en: Establish component decomposition for RAG evaluation rather than collapsing the pipeline into one end-to-end score.

locator.en: Chapter 4 "Evaluate AI Systems" → "Design Your Evaluation Pipeline" (pp. 200-207), especially evaluating all components, guidelines, methods, and data

purpose.en: Apply the repository's general evaluation discipline to each RAG component and the full system.

locator.en: RAG evaluation metrics documentation for context/retrieval and generation-oriented metrics

purpose.en: Inspect concrete metric definitions as examples while keeping metric choice tied to the product/evaluation contract rather than the framework.

text.en: Take five bad Knowledge Assistant answers and classify each as retrieval miss, ranking/context-selection failure, insufficient/noisy context, unfaithful generation, answer-quality failure despite sufficient context, or evaluation-label problem.
Produce a RAG evaluation record with retrieval, context, generation, end-to-end, evaluator-provenance, failure-taxonomy, and regression evidence for two system configurations.

items.en: Hold generation fixed while changing retrieval and verify which metrics/failures move.
Supply an oracle/relevant context for selected cases to test whether generation succeeds when retrieval is removed as the failure source.
Calibrate at least one model-based evaluator against a small human-reviewed sample and record disagreements.
A versioned evaluation set and system configuration are recorded.
Retrieval evidence is separated from context and generation evidence.
Important failures are attributed to a component with inspectable examples.
Model-based evaluator provenance and calibration are recorded when used.
Production or project failures become regression cases.
The final architecture/release decision does not rely on a single aggregate RAG score.

body.en: Redesign the evaluation for a different RAG domain with different relevance, citation, freshness, or abstention requirements and explain which metrics or labels must change.
AI system changes are difficult to reason about without repeatable evidence for quality, failures, variance, latency, and cost.

diagnostic.en: Explain how you would compare two system configurations without changing the evaluation data or success criteria after seeing the results.

locator.en: Evaluation lesson sections covering overall evaluation, per-class evaluation, slices, behavioral testing, and online evaluation.

purpose.en: Patch the experiment-design discipline needed to make system comparisons meaningful.

diagnostic.en: Distinguish a unit test, integration test, system test, and regression test using one AI application example.

locator.en: Testing lesson sections "Types of tests" and "How should we test?".

purpose.en: Patch the testing vocabulary and regression mindset used by the evaluation harness.

items.en: Define evaluation criteria from a product or system objective.
Evaluate system components separately from end-to-end behavior.
Build and version representative evaluation data.
Combine deterministic, semantic, retrieval, and agent evaluation where appropriate.
Measure repeated-run variance for stochastic systems.
Perform failure analysis using categories and slices.
Turn production failures into regression cases.
Define release gates using explicit quality, latency, and cost constraints.

tasks.en: Design an evaluation plan for a prompt, retrieval, or model change without relying only on average answer quality.
Explain how to separate retrieval failure from generation failure in a RAG system.
Explain when an LLM judge needs calibration and what it should be calibrated against.
Decide what evidence would block a release.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory evaluation material only if the learner can produce a concrete evaluation design with component metrics, representative data, failure analysis, repeated runs when needed, and release criteria.

locator.en: Chapter 3 "Evaluation Methodology" and Chapter 4 section "Design Your Evaluation Pipeline"

purpose.en: Learn exact/model-based/comparative evaluation and connect evaluation criteria, methods, data, and system components.

locator.en: Evaluation lesson; overall, per-class, slices, behavioral testing, and online evaluation sections

purpose.en: Connect aggregate metrics to failure analysis and production evaluation.

text.en: Create an evaluation matrix for one existing AI feature covering objective, unit, dataset, metric, failure categories, latency, cost, and release threshold.
Complete the evaluation-harness lab and produce a versioned comparison plus release decision.

items.en: Run the same stochastic system multiple times and measure outcome variance.
Compare aggregate metrics with slice-level or failure-category analysis.
Calibrate one model-based judge against a small human-reviewed set.
Produce a versioned evaluation set and rationale for its coverage.
Compare two system configurations using explicit metrics.
Separate at least one component-level failure from an end-to-end failure.
Analyze failure categories or slices rather than only aggregate scores.
Define a release gate that includes quality and at least one operational constraint.

body.en: Redesign the evaluation for an agent workflow with tool calls, including trajectory or tool-use evidence rather than only final-answer quality.

A reliable AI system must decide when evidence is sufficient to answer and when it should abstain, fall back, or escalate. Useful trust decisions require validated signals, held-out threshold selection, and explicit risk–coverage trade-offs rather than model self-reported confidence alone.

diagnostic.en: Given confidence bins and observed accuracies, explain whether the scores are calibrated, why one example cannot establish calibration, and why threshold selection belongs on validation rather than test data.

locator.en: Section 2 "Definitions" plus the reliability-diagram and Expected Calibration Error discussion

purpose.en: Patch only the probability and calibration reasoning needed to interpret confidence or risk signals and select policies without test leakage.

items.en: Define what abstention means for the product and what fallback or escalation follows it.
Define answer risk, coverage, and the cost of a wrong answer versus an unnecessary abstention.
Choose candidate uncertainty or evidence signals from observed failure modes.
Validate whether a signal separates safer from riskier cases on held-out data.
Select a threshold or policy on validation data rather than the final test set.
Produce a risk–coverage curve or equivalent threshold-sweep evidence.
Measure false abstention, unsafe answered cases, fallback success, and important slices.
Test the policy under distribution, freshness, retrieval, or evidence shift.
Treat model self-evaluation as a candidate signal to validate rather than a calibrated probability by default.
Make a release or architecture decision from the measured trade-off.

tasks.en: Given a Knowledge Assistant with a confidence-like score, design evidence that would show whether the score is useful for answer versus abstain decisions.
Explain why a policy that abstains on almost every case can have low answered-case error while still being a poor product.
Describe how validation and held-out test data should be used when selecting an abstention threshold.
Define at least two candidate signals and one fallback behavior for insufficient evidence.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design a selective-answer policy, preserve validation/test separation, evaluate risk and coverage together, and reject unvalidated confidence signals.

locator.en: Sections 1 "Introduction", 2 "Selective Prediction Problem Formulation", and 5 "Coverage Accuracy"

purpose.en: Establish the reject-option formulation, coverage, selective risk, and the risk–coverage trade-off without requiring the SelectiveNet model itself.

locator.en: Section 2 "Definitions", "Reliability Diagrams", and "Expected Calibration Error (ECE)"

purpose.en: Distinguish predictive accuracy from calibration and learn how empirical reliability is inspected over groups of comparable cases.

locator.en: Calibration results and Section 3 "From Calibration to Knowing What You Know", including P(True) self-evaluation experiments

purpose.en: Treat model self-evaluation as a measurable signal whose calibration and task transfer must be validated rather than trusted by label.

text.en: Label a small slice of existing Knowledge Assistant cases as answerable, insufficient-evidence, or needs-review, then predict which available signals should separate the groups before computing results.
Compare at least two answerability or risk signals, select an answer/abstain/fallback policy on validation data, and evaluate the chosen policy once on a held-out test set.

items.en: Sweep a threshold and report coverage together with answered-case risk or quality.
Compare at least two candidate signals or policies rather than assuming a self-reported confidence score is meaningful.
Create an insufficient-evidence, stale, or shifted slice and inspect whether the selected policy still behaves safely.
Measure false or unnecessary abstention and unsafe answered cases at the selected operating point.
Exercise the fallback or escalation path and measure whether it actually resolves the abstained cases.
Evaluation data includes versioned answerability or risk labels and a documented validation/test split.
The no-abstention baseline is preserved.
Candidate signals and their provenance are recorded.
Threshold or policy selection uses validation data and does not tune on the final test set.
Risk and coverage are reported together through a curve or equivalent sweep.
False or unnecessary abstention, unsafe answered cases, and fallback outcome are measured.
At least one shifted, stale, or insufficient-evidence slice is analyzed.
At least two candidate signals or policies are compared.
The release or architecture decision explains the chosen trade-off and what evidence would change it.

body.en: Redesign the answer-versus-abstain policy for a domain with different error costs or fallback options, such as support triage, compliance review, or code change approval.
Add model-directed autonomy only when fixed workflows cannot satisfy the task well enough and the measured benefit justifies the added cost and failure surface.

diagnostic.en: Describe a tool schema, what the model chooses versus what application code executes, and one validation boundary for tool arguments.

locator.en: Building block: The augmented LLM; Appendix 2: Prompt engineering your tools.

purpose.en: Patch the model-to-tool interface needed before comparing agentic control strategies.

diagnostic.en: Explain how a regression test differs from a happy-path example and where an end-to-end agent test belongs relative to unit tests.

locator.en: Testing lesson sections "Types of tests" and system/regression testing discussion.

purpose.en: Patch the testing discipline required to compare workflow and agent failures on the same task set.

items.en: Distinguish workflows with predefined code paths from agents that dynamically direct their process and tool use.
Start from the simplest viable architecture and use failure analysis to justify additional autonomy.
Select between chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, evaluator-optimizer, and agent loops based on task structure.
Compare workflow and agentic implementations on the same task set.
Define stop conditions, tool boundaries, traces, and measurable success criteria for autonomous behavior.
Reject agentic complexity when it does not produce enough measured value.

tasks.en: Given a task, decide whether one model call, a deterministic workflow, or an agent is appropriate and explain why.
Name the failure evidence that would justify increasing autonomy.
Explain what new failure modes, cost, and debugging difficulty an autonomous loop introduces.
Define a stop condition and a measurable task-success criterion.

pass_condition.en: Skip guided material only if the learner can select the simplest viable architecture from task structure and defend autonomy with same-set evaluation evidence.

locator.en: Sections: "What are agents?", "When (and when not) to use agents", "Building blocks, workflows, and agents", and "Combining and customizing these patterns"

purpose.en: Distinguish fixed workflows from agents, learn common workflow patterns, and use measured complexity as the selection principle.

text.en: Classify three familiar product tasks by whether their steps and branches are predictable, then choose the simplest architecture for each.
Compare a simple baseline with a more autonomous design on the same versioned task set.

items.en: Measure task success, model calls/steps, latency, cost, and failure types for baseline and agentic versions.
Remove autonomy from one design and identify whether task quality actually degrades.
Produce a simple baseline architecture before introducing an agent.
Show failure analysis that motivates any additional autonomy.
Compare baseline and agentic variants on the same task set.
Record cost/latency/debuggability as well as quality.
Define stop conditions and bounded tool permissions.
Make an explicit keep-workflow or use-agent decision from evidence.

body.en: Compare one task with known fixed subtasks and one whose subtasks depend on intermediate environment/tool results; choose and defend a different architecture when appropriate.

Multi-step and interruptible agent workflows need explicit durable execution state so they can resume correctly after failures, avoid duplicated side effects, and project only the state needed for the next model call.

items.en: Distinguish durable execution state, current model context, event history, external environment state, observability data, and long-term memory.
Define an explicit serializable state schema instead of relying on conversation text as implicit control state.
Identify persisted values, derived values, and values that should not be stored.
Define legal state transitions, terminal states, and meaningful checkpoint or event boundaries.
Resume after interruption or process loss from durable state rather than restarting the workflow.
Prevent completed side effects from being duplicated after replay or resume.
Use durable run or correlation identifiers to connect state transitions and external actions.
Inspect checkpoint or event history to explain how a run reached its current state.
Version state and handle one compatible or breaking state-schema change.
Project only the state required for the next inference into model context.

tasks.en: For a multi-step Knowledge Assistant workflow, classify each piece of information as execution state, event history, current model context, observability data, external environment state, or long-term memory.
Define a state transition table and identify where a durable checkpoint belongs.
Explain how the workflow resumes after a crash that occurs after an external side effect succeeds but before the next model call.
Explain why rereading the transcript is not a sufficient recovery contract.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can design explicit resumable state, choose checkpoint boundaries, and prevent duplicate side effects under replay.

locator.en: Section "Core Concepts", especially the distinction among Session, State, and Memory

purpose.en: Establish a clean boundary between one conversation thread, mutable session state, and cross-session memory.

locator.en: Sections "What is session.state?", "Key Characteristics of State", and "How State is Updated: Recommended Methods"

purpose.en: Study serializable mutable state and tracked state updates as one concrete implementation model.

locator.en: Sections "Step 3: Design your state", "What belongs in state?", "Keep state raw, format prompts on-demand", the interrupt/checkpointer example, and "Advanced considerations — Node granularity trade-offs"

purpose.en: Learn to keep raw execution data in state, derive prompt/context views on demand, and connect checkpoint granularity to recovery behavior.

locator.en: Documentation overview describing durable execution and resuming where execution left off after crashes, network failures, or infrastructure outages

purpose.en: Ground recovery semantics in a production durable-execution model without requiring Temporal.

locator.en: Sections "The long-running agent problem", "Incremental progress", and "Getting up to speed"

purpose.en: See why context compaction alone is insufficient and how durable progress artifacts allow fresh contexts to continue work.

text.en: Take one existing Knowledge Assistant tool workflow and rewrite its implicit progress as an explicit state schema plus transition table.
Add durable state to an interruptible multi-step Knowledge Assistant workflow, inject a crash after a completed step, then resume without duplicating the completed side effect.

items.en: Crash the workflow after an external action succeeds but before the following step and verify resume behavior.
Move a checkpoint boundary and measure repeated work or duplicate-side-effect risk.
Remove a derived field from persisted state and verify it can be reconstructed safely.
Inject stale, corrupt, or incompatible state and verify detection and recovery behavior.
Migrate one persisted state schema and exercise an in-flight old-version run.
A versioned state schema distinguishes persisted, derived, and intentionally unstored values.
A transition table or equivalent defines legal transitions and terminal states.
Durable checkpoint or event boundaries are explicit.
An injected interruption resumes from persisted state rather than restarting the whole workflow.
Replay or resume does not duplicate a previously completed side effect.
Correlation or idempotency identifiers connect persisted state to external actions where needed.
One stale, corrupt, or incompatible-state case is handled explicitly.
One state-schema migration decision covers existing persisted runs.
The learner explains why transcript-only continuity is insufficient for this workflow.

body.en: Redesign the state and recovery contract for a different interruptible workflow whose side effects and checkpoint costs differ from the Knowledge Assistant.

Cross-session memory can improve continuity and personalization, but uncontrolled retention creates stale facts, harmful recall, privacy and isolation failures, and context noise. Engineers need explicit admission, retrieval, provenance, lifecycle, and evaluation policies.

items.en: Distinguish execution state, current context, session history, product corpus retrieval, and long-term agent memory.
Justify why a piece of information should be persisted across sessions instead of retained only in current context or recomputed.
Define memory scope, schema, provenance, timestamps or freshness, write admission, and retrieval rules.
Choose a storage and retrieval mechanism from the memory type rather than defaulting to vector search.
Retrieve memories selectively in a new session and project only relevant memories into current context.
Measure whether memory improves the target task relative to a no-memory baseline.
Detect irrelevant, stale, conflicting, false, or incorrectly scoped memories.
Support correction, update, and deletion or forgetting behavior.
Prevent cross-user, cross-workspace, or cross-scope leakage where identities exist.
Reject memory complexity when measured benefit does not justify cost or harmful recall.

tasks.en: Classify examples such as current workflow step, user preference, retrieved document chunk, durable project convention, and raw transcript as state, memory candidate, context candidate, corpus data, or neither.
Define a write/admission policy for one cross-session Knowledge Assistant memory use case.
Explain how stale, conflicting, corrected, and deleted memories should behave on a later session.
Design a no-memory versus memory evaluation that can reveal both benefit and harmful recall.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can define a scoped memory lifecycle, evaluate it across sessions, and reject unbounded retention or unvalidated recall.

locator.en: Section "Core Concepts", especially Session, State, and Memory

purpose.en: Establish the distinction between single-thread history/state and searchable information spanning past sessions.

locator.en: Sections "Memory: Long-term knowledge with MemoryService" and "The MemoryService role"

purpose.en: Study explicit memory ingestion and later search as a concrete cross-session memory interface.

locator.en: Section "Context engineering for long-horizon tasks", especially "Structured note-taking"

purpose.en: Separate persistent external notes or memory from the smaller subset loaded into the current context.

locator.en: Persistence overview and the "Checkpointer vs. store" distinction

purpose.en: Compare thread-scoped checkpoint state with application-defined storage that can span threads.

locator.en: Sections 1 "Introduction", 2 "MemGPT (MemoryGPT)", 2.1 "Main context (prompt tokens)", 2.2 "Queue Manager", 3.1 "MemGPT for conversational agents", and 3.1.1 "Deep memory retrieval task"

purpose.en: Study finite current context versus persistent external storage and the need to evaluate retrieval of older information without adopting the architecture as a default.

text.en: Review ten pieces of information from the Knowledge Assistant and decide which should be forgotten, remain session-local, enter product corpus storage, or become a scoped long-term memory; justify each admission decision.
Add one justified cross-session memory use case, compare no-memory with at least two memory policies, and test stale, conflicting, correction, deletion, and isolation behavior.

items.en: Compare no memory, simple structured memory, and an alternative write/read policy on the same cross-session cases.
Inject an irrelevant memory and measure whether it is incorrectly retrieved or influences the answer.
Age or supersede a memory and test freshness/conflict behavior.
Correct and delete a memory, then verify later sessions do not continue using the obsolete value.
Attempt cross-user or cross-scope retrieval where identity exists.
Compare a simple keyed lookup with semantic retrieval when the memory type supports both.
A versioned memory schema defines scope, provenance, timestamps or freshness, and content type.
Write or admission criteria explicitly reject information that should not be persisted.
Retrieval criteria explain when memory is searched and when candidates enter model context.
Multi-session evaluation preserves a no-memory baseline and compares at least two memory policies.
Task benefit is reported together with harmful or irrelevant recall, latency, and context/token cost.
Stale and conflicting memories are tested.
Correction or update and deletion or forgetting are verified in later sessions.
Cross-user or cross-scope isolation is tested where identity exists.
A context-projection trace shows exactly which memories influenced the model call.
The final decision records whether memory is worth keeping for this product need.

body.en: Redesign the memory policy for a different application whose retention, scope, privacy, or freshness requirements differ materially.

Explicit planning is useful when task structure depends on intermediate results, but planner scaffolding should remain inspectable, stateful, revisable, and removable when it does not improve outcomes enough to justify its cost.

items.en: Decide when explicit planning is useful versus unnecessary overhead.
Represent a plan as an inspectable external artifact rather than hidden reasoning.
Define goals, constraints, success criteria, steps or dependencies, blockers, assumptions, and invalidation triggers.
Choose plan granularity that avoids both under-specification and brittle low-level over-specification.
Persist plan status in durable execution state.
Update plan progress from tool or environment results.
Detect invalidated assumptions or blocked dependencies.
Replan from observed evidence instead of blindly continuing the original plan.
Define termination and success conditions before execution.
Compare no-plan, static-plan, and adaptive-plan variants on the same task set.
Reject planner scaffolding when it does not create enough measurable value.

tasks.en: Given a Knowledge Assistant task, decide whether direct execution, a static plan, or adaptive planning is appropriate and explain what task property justifies the choice.
Design a plan schema that can survive a process restart and be updated without relying on hidden reasoning.
Describe one condition that should invalidate the current plan and what evidence should trigger replanning.
Define how you would prove that a planner is helping rather than merely adding steps.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can externalize plan structure, persist it in state, replan from environment evidence, and compare planning variants on the same task set.

locator.en: Sections "Workflow: Orchestrator-workers", "Agents", "Combining and customizing these patterns", and "Summary"

purpose.en: Distinguish predictable workflow decomposition from dynamic task decomposition and keep complexity tied to measurable need.

locator.en: Sections "Scaling to full-stack coding" → "The architecture" (Planner), "Iterating on the harness", and "Removing the sprint construct"

purpose.en: Study planner granularity, under-scoping, cascading assumptions, and ablation of planner/decomposition scaffolding as model capability changes.

locator.en: Sections "What is an agent?", "Configuring instructions", "Orchestration", and "Single-agent systems"

purpose.en: Ground planning in executable workflow control, explicit steps/branches, completion conditions, and single-agent-first architecture.

text.en: Take one stateful Knowledge Assistant workflow and externalize a minimal plan with explicit assumptions, dependencies, completion criteria, and replanning triggers.
Compare no-plan, static-plan, and adaptive-plan variants on the same task set, inject one invalidated assumption, and preserve the replanning trace.

items.en: Remove explicit planning and measure whether task success or failure attribution changes.
Compare a coarse plan with an over-detailed plan to identify brittleness from premature assumptions.
Invalidate one dependency or assumption mid-run and verify the plan updates from observed evidence.
Measure plan churn, redundant steps, tool calls, latency, and cost across variants.
A versioned plan schema records goals, constraints, success criteria, dependencies or steps, status, assumptions, and replanning triggers.
The plan is persisted in durable state or an artifact referenced by state.
A no-plan baseline is preserved.
Static and adaptive planning variants are compared on the same task set.
At least one changed condition or invalidated assumption triggers an inspectable plan revision.
Task success is reported with steps or tool calls, latency, cost where measurable, and unnecessary replanning.
The learner records whether planning should be kept, simplified, or removed.

body.en: Redesign the planning strategy for a task with a different dependency structure and uncertainty profile, then justify a different plan granularity or no-plan decision if appropriate.

Agent narration is not proof that a task succeeded. Reliable systems verify real environment state, artifacts, tests, authoritative data, or calibrated judgments and use failed verification to repair, retry, replan, abstain, or escalate.

diagnostic.en: Explain the difference between a happy-path example, a regression test, an integration or end-to-end check, and an assertion against real environment state.

locator.en: Testing lesson sections "Types of tests" and system/regression testing discussion

purpose.en: Patch only the testing discipline needed to design deterministic verification and reproduce failures without requiring the full software-testing route.

items.en: Define verifiable success criteria before execution.
Map each criterion to the strongest practical verifier.
Prefer deterministic or environment evidence over agent narration when available.
Insert verification at useful intermediate or terminal boundaries.
Distinguish verification failure from execution, planning, state, and genuine task failure.
Use failed verification to trigger repair, retry, replan, abstention, or human escalation.
Seed known defects and measure whether the verifier detects them.
Measure false positives and false negatives for verifier logic that can fail.
Calibrate model-based graders against human judgment when they are required.
Version verifier logic, rubrics, and provenance.
Compare task outcomes with and without the verification loop.
Remove expensive verification stages when they no longer provide measurable lift.

tasks.en: Given a claimed Knowledge Assistant outcome, identify which facts can be checked against environment state, executable tests, authoritative data, a model grader, or human review.
Explain why a successful transcript is not equivalent to a successful environment outcome.
Seed one defect and design a verifier that should detect it.
Describe how you would measure and calibrate a model-based grader if deterministic checks are insufficient.

pass_condition.en: Skip introductory material only if the learner can define outcome-based verification, detect seeded defects, measure verifier errors, and route failed verification into a concrete recovery action.

locator.en: Sections "The structure of an evaluation", "Types of graders for agents", "Design the eval harness and graders", and guidance on transcript versus final environment outcome

purpose.en: Separate trajectory from outcome and choose deterministic, model-based, or human graders based on the property being checked.

locator.en: Sections "Workflow: Prompt chaining", "Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer", "Agents", and "Appendix 1: Coding agents"

purpose.en: Connect intermediate checks, evaluator-optimizer loops, environment feedback, and objective tests to agent execution.

locator.en: Sections "Frontend design: making subjective quality gradable", "Scaling to full-stack coding" → "The architecture" (Evaluator), and "Removing the sprint construct"

purpose.en: Study explicit grading criteria, Playwright/environment verification, evaluator calibration, and ablation of evaluator overhead.

locator.en: Abstract and method framing comparing unsupported self-correction with tool-interactive critique

purpose.en: Reinforce that external feedback can provide stronger correction evidence than unconstrained self-critique.

locator.en: Abstract and benchmark formulation using real repository issues and test suites to grade patches

purpose.en: Ground verification in outcome artifacts and executable environment checks rather than plausible-looking trajectories.

text.en: Take one Knowledge Assistant success criterion and replace a narrative or model-only check with a deterministic, environment, or authoritative-data verifier where possible.
Build a verifier inventory, seed at least one defect, record successful and failed verification traces, and compare the same task set with and without the verification loop.

items.en: Seed a defect that should be caught by a deterministic or environment verifier and measure detection.
Remove one verifier stage and identify which failures become invisible.
Introduce a verifier false positive or false negative and trace the downstream recovery consequence.
If a model grader is used, compare its judgments with a human-reviewed calibration sample.
Compare verification overhead and task outcome before and after adding the verification loop.
Versioned success criteria exist before execution.
Each criterion is mapped to a concrete verifier and evidence source.
At least one deterministic or environment verifier is present.
At least one seeded defect is tested.
Successful and failed verification traces are preserved.
Failure attribution distinguishes planning, execution, state, verifier, and genuine task failures.
False-positive or false-negative evidence is reported where the verifier can be wrong.
Model graders, if used, include rubric/version/provenance and human calibration evidence.
Verification overhead is measured.
The learner records whether each verifier stage should be kept, simplified, or removed.

body.en: Redesign the verification hierarchy for a task where correctness is more subjective or where environment checks are expensive, and justify where model or human grading becomes necessary.
LLM inputs can influence model behavior in unintended ways, so privileged actions and data access must remain protected even when the model or external content is adversarially influenced.

diagnostic.en: Explain why an authenticated user identity and authorization policy must be checked by application code rather than inferred from model text.

locator.en: Prevention and Mitigation Strategies, especially privilege control and human approval for high-risk operations.

purpose.en: Patch the identity-versus-model boundary needed to understand deterministic authorization.

diagnostic.en: Given a read-only tool and an admin export tool, assign least-privilege permissions and state where enforcement occurs.

locator.en: Prevention and Mitigation Strategies, especially least privilege and privilege control.

purpose.en: Patch the tool-permission model needed for the trust-boundary lab.

diagnostic.en: Explain the difference between a model proposing a tool invocation and application code authorizing and executing it.

locator.en: Building block: The augmented LLM; Appendix 2: Prompt engineering your tools.

purpose.en: Patch the model/tool interaction needed to reason about compromised tool requests.

items.en: Distinguish direct from indirect prompt injection and explain why RAG or fine-tuning does not eliminate the risk.
Identify trusted policy, untrusted external content, model-controlled output, and privileged action boundaries.
Enforce authorization and least privilege outside the model.
Use human approval or other deterministic controls for high-risk actions where appropriate.
Design adversarial tests for retrieved content, tools, and authorization boundaries.
Explain the limits of prompt-only or filtering-only mitigations.

tasks.en: Explain direct and indirect prompt injection using one realistic system example each.
Draw the trust boundaries for a RAG system that can call privileged tools.
Explain where authorization must be enforced if the model proposes a forbidden action.
Describe an adversarial test that proves a trust boundary still holds after a model is influenced.

pass_condition.en: Skip guided material only if the learner can threat-model both direct and indirect injection and implement deterministic authorization that remains correct under simulated compromised model output.

locator.en: Sections: "Types of Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities", "Prevention and Mitigation Strategies", and "Example Attack Scenarios"

purpose.en: Establish direct/indirect injection risks, impact, least-privilege controls, human approval, external-content segregation, and adversarial testing.

locator.en: Chapter 5 "Defensive Prompt Engineering" — Jailbreaking and Prompt Injection, and Defenses Against Prompt Attacks

purpose.en: Connect prompt attacks to application-level defensive design in foundation-model systems.

text.en: Draw trust boundaries for a retrieval system with one read-only tool and one privileged tool; label every model-controlled or external-data edge as untrusted.
Complete the trust-boundary lab so privileged tool execution is blocked even when model output is simulated as compromised.

items.en: Add a simulated indirect injection to retrieved content and verify privileged action controls still hold.
Change the authenticated user's permission set and verify authorization follows identity/policy rather than model text.
Explain direct and indirect prompt injection.
Produce a trust-boundary diagram for an LLM application with external content or tools.
Implement authorization outside the model and pass adversarial boundary tests.
Show least-privilege or approval handling for a high-risk action.
Explain why prompt instructions or filtering alone are insufficient as the authorization mechanism.

body.en: Threat-model an email assistant that can read messages and send replies; identify indirect-injection paths, privileged actions, approval points, and deterministic controls.
